title: Family caregiving operates as unpaid social infrastructure while shifting health, work, money, and social costs onto caregivers
source_unit: Pew Research Center American Trends Panel survey of US adults with aging parents or spouses/partners

denominator.unit: US adults surveyed; 1,193 identify as caregivers for an aging parent, spouse, or partner

parent_caregiver.unit: percent of all US adults identifying as a caregiver for a parent age 65 or older

spouse_partner_caregiver.unit: percent of all US adults identifying as a caregiver for an aging spouse or partner

among_people_with_aging_parent.unit: percent identifying as a caregiver among adults with a parent age 65 or older

among_people_with_aging_spouse.unit: percent identifying as a caregiver among adults with an aging spouse or partner

observations.method: Pew American Trends Panel survey with separate caregiver universes for aging parents and spouses/partners; caregiver identity is self-reported.
observations.uncertainty: Self-identifying as a caregiver does not measure hours, necessity, care quality, paid alternatives, or whether the same person provides care continuously.
observations.subgroup: US adults overall and adults with an aging parent or spouse/partner; parent and spouse/partner caregiver universes are separate.
observations.counterinterpretation: Caregiver identification can reflect closeness, obligation, occasional coordination, intensive hands-on care, or combinations of these; the headline share is not a burden rate.

observations.period: September 2-8, 2025; caregiving tasks and household role

denominator.unit: Pew survey respondents identifying as caregivers for an aging parent, spouse, or partner; task-specific valid universes vary

regular_parent_care_tasks.value: about 68% of parent caregivers regularly help with at least one of errands/housework/home repairs, health-care management, financial management, or personal care

regular_spouse_care_tasks.value: about 66% of spouse/partner caregivers regularly help with at least one of the listed tasks

care_tasks.value: tasks include appointments and medication, bills and budgeting, errands and repairs, and bathing or dressing

observations.method: Pew self-report of regular caregiving tasks; parent and spouse/partner task categories are not pooled into one intensity index.
observations.uncertainty: Task presence does not establish frequency, duration, skill, financial cost, substitution, or whether public or paid care was available.
observations.subgroup: US adults caring for an aging parent or spouse/partner.
observations.counterinterpretation: Family care can preserve independence and relationships while still transferring administrative, medical, and time work into the household.

observations.period: September 2-8, 2025; reported caregiver effects and inequality

denominator.unit: Pew caregiver subgroups with regular-task and impact responses; item-specific valid denominators

lower_income_caregiving.value: 39% of lower-income adults with an aging parent or partner identify as caregivers, versus 23% of middle-income and 16% of upper-income adults

parent_caregiver_negative_effects.value: parent caregivers report more negative than positive effects on emotional well-being, physical health, job/career, financial situation, and social life, while relationship effects tend more positive

gender_emotional_effect.value: 47% of women versus 30% of men caring for a parent report a negative emotional-well-being impact
gender_emotional_effect.unit: percent among parent caregivers with the relevant response

gender_physical_effect.value: 38% of women versus 26% of men report a negative physical-health impact when caring for a parent
gender_physical_effect.unit: percent among parent caregivers with the relevant response

observations.method: Descriptive Pew subgroup comparisons by income and gender; the cross-sectional survey does not establish that caregiving caused the reported effects.
observations.uncertainty: Income, gender, health, family structure, care intensity, prior relationship, and selection into caregiving are entangled; impact questions are retrospective or current self-reports.
observations.subgroup: US adults caring for an aging parent, with separate income and gender comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Positive relationship meaning can coexist with negative health, work, money, or social effects; caregiving is not adequately described as either burden or benefit alone.

boundary: This record establishes family-caregiving prevalence, tasks, income/gender differences, and reported cross-domain effects. It does not establish exact hours, paid-care substitution, adequacy, household financial recovery, health causation, policy receipt, trust, political action, or caregiver exit.
